newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends up in Europe as mark retains weak bias.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends up in Europe as mark retains weak bias.

text.p: The dollar closed higher here, underpinned by mark weakness in the wake of the European Union's agreement on Friday on a post-monetary union stability pact.

The stability pact has refuelled optimism the single currency project will start on schedule, analysts said. It also increases the chances of a broader EMU, including Italy and Spain. As a result, the mark weakened on its European crosses, helping the dollar to retain the bulk of its weekend gains.
"The weekend news argues in favour of a stronger dollar into the end of the year," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America.
At 1551 GMT the dollar traded at 1.4439/49 marks, off its session peak at 1.5577 but up from 1.5454/66 in late European trading on Friday.
Dollar/yen was also firmer at 113.95/114.00, off a session high at 114.13 but up from 113.77/83 at the previous close.
The agreement on long-term fiscal austerity will lower the European interest rate horizon and buoy both the dollar and the yen against the European bloc, analysts said.
Hawkins said the focus was now on the outlook for lower rates in Portugal and Sweden which were likely to follow Spain's cut last week, and on possible easing in Italy and France.

The boost to EMU optimism also knocked the Swiss franc lower, which traditionally benefits from single currency uncertainty. The Swiss National Bank's reiteration on Friday that it would keep monetary policy loose also continued to weigh on the franc, traders said.
Dollar/Swiss was 1.3265/72 francs from 1.3626/31, while mark/Swiss stood at 85.39/42 from 85.21/24.
Traders were cautious though to push the dollar higher ahead of Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting even though few expect an interest rate change at this last meeting of the year.
"It looks as if the market is starting to wind down for Christmas, so the ranges are likely to become smaller and smaller," said a trader at a German bank.

The mark was weighed down further by news of a drop in the November business sentiment index of Germany's Ifo research institute to 96.9 from 97.3. Ifo said that while growth would pick up to 2.5 percent next year, unemployment will remain high and inflation will remain subdued at 1.5 percent.
The institute said the Bundesbank was unlikely to change its official discount and Lombard rates, but it may lower its key repurchase rate again.
The Bundesbank council meets Thursday and holds a press briefing to announce its 1997 M3 money supply growth targets.
Dollar/yen perked up amid demand from U.S. names. Dealers also noted talk of demand out of Japan to buy dollar calls with strikes of 115 yen for three-month and 120 for six-months calls.

U.S. industrial production rose by a robust 0.9 percent in November, the largest rise in nine months and against 0.6 percent forecast. The Fed said half of the rise was due to a rebound in General Motors auto production after a strike. Capacity utilisation rose to 83.3 from 82.9 in October.
